# ECG Means

> Independent, clinician-reviewed plain-English explanations of the phrases printed on ECG/EKG reports. Every page is written and reviewed by Dr. Faisal Irshad, MBBS (PMDC 54440-S) and states plainly whether a finding is usually harmless, context-dependent, needs clinician review, or warrants prompt care. Educational only; not a substitute for the clinician who ordered the test.

## ECG Report Phrases
- [ECG Report Phrases Explained](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-report-phrases/): The wording the machine prints — abnormal ECG, borderline ECG, septal infarct, nonspecific T wave abnormality — and what each line really means.
- [Abnormal ECG: What It Means on Your Report](https://www.ecgmeans.com/abnormal-ecg/): 'Abnormal ECG' printed on your report? Learn what the machine is flagging, the common harmless causes, the serious ones, and what usually happens next.
- [Anterior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/anterior-infarct-age-undetermined/): What 'anterior infarct, age undetermined' or 'possible anterior infarct' means on an ECG printout, why it is often a false alarm, and which test settles it.
- [Anteroseptal Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/anteroseptal-infarct/): 'Anteroseptal infarct, age undetermined' means Q waves or lost R waves across V1–V4. Learn why lead placement and body build often mimic it and what confirms it.
- [Borderline ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/borderline-ecg/): A 'borderline ECG' sits between normal and abnormal. See which small findings trigger it, why it is usually harmless, and when it deserves follow-up.
- [Early Repolarization on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/early-repolarization/): Early repolarization is a common ECG variant in young, fit people. Learn what it looks like, why it is usually benign, and the rare situations where it matters.
- [Inferior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/inferior-infarct-age-undetermined/): 'Inferior infarct, age undetermined' means Q waves in II, III and aVF that can follow an old heart attack. Learn why it is often a false alarm.
- [Lateral Infarct: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/lateral-infarct/): A lateral infarct means Q waves or changes in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6). Learn what it suggests about the side wall of the heart and how it is confirmed.
- [Left Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-axis-deviation/): Left axis deviation means the heart's overall electrical direction points further left than usual. See the numbers, the causes and why it is rarely a problem alone.
- [Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-ventricular-hypertrophy/): 'Possible left ventricular hypertrophy' or 'voltage criteria for LVH' on your ECG means tall QRS complexes. Learn why the ECG over-calls it and what confirms it.
- [Low Voltage QRS: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/low-voltage-qrs/): Low voltage QRS means the main spikes on your ECG are smaller than usual. Learn the criteria, the harmless and the important causes, and the usual follow-up.
- [Nonspecific T Wave Abnormality: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/nonspecific-t-wave-abnormality/): 'Nonspecific T wave abnormality' is among the commonest ECG printout lines. Find out what T waves are, why they flatten, and when it matters.
- [Pericarditis on an ECG: What It Shows](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pericarditis-ecg/): Pericarditis causes widespread, concave ST elevation and PR depression on the ECG. Learn how doctors tell it apart from a heart attack and what the stages look like.
- [Poor R Wave Progression: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/poor-r-wave-progression/): Poor R wave progression means the R waves don't grow normally across the chest leads. It is usually lead placement or body build — here's how it is sorted out.
- [Possible Left Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-atrial-enlargement/): 'Possible left atrial enlargement' is based on the shape of your P wave. Learn how reliable it is, what causes a big left atrium, and why an echo is the real test.
- [Possible Right Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-atrial-enlargement/): 'Possible right atrial enlargement' is read from a tall, peaked P wave (P pulmonale). Learn what causes it and why an echocardiogram is the real test.
- [Right Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-axis-deviation/): Right axis deviation means the heart's electrical direction points further right than normal. See the causes, when it is a normal variant, and when it matters.
- [Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-ventricular-hypertrophy/): Right ventricular hypertrophy on an ECG shows as a tall R wave in V1 and right axis deviation. Learn what thickens the right ventricle and why an echo confirms it.
- [Septal Infarct on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/septal-infarct/): 'Septal infarct, age undetermined' is one of the most common false alarms on ECG reports. Learn what the machine saw, why it is often wrong, and how it is checked.

## Heart Rhythms
- [Heart Rhythms on the ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/heart-rhythms/): Sinus rhythm and its variants, junctional and ventricular rhythms, and the extra-beat patterns bigeminy and trigeminy.
- [Accelerated Junctional Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/accelerated-junctional-rhythm/): Accelerated junctional rhythm is a junctional rhythm at 60–100 bpm. See how it differs from sinus rhythm, the classic causes, and how it is managed.
- [Atrial Fibrillation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-fibrillation/): Atrial fibrillation is an irregular heart rhythm with no clear P waves on the ECG. Learn how it is recognised, why it raises stroke risk, and how it is treated.
- [Atrial Flutter: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-flutter/): Atrial flutter shows a sawtooth pattern on the ECG with a fast, often regular pulse. Learn how it differs from atrial fibrillation and why it raises stroke risk.
- [Atrial Tachycardia: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-tachycardia/): Atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm from a focus in the atria, with abnormal P waves before each beat. Learn how it differs from sinus tachycardia and SVT.
- [Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/bigeminy/): Bigeminy means every other heartbeat is an extra beat, usually a PVC. Learn what it looks and feels like, the common triggers, and when it needs investigation.
- [Ectopic Atrial Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ectopic-atrial-rhythm/): An ectopic atrial rhythm starts outside the sinus node, so the P waves look unusual. Learn why it is often a benign variant and when it needs checking.
- [Idioventricular Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/idioventricular-rhythm/): Idioventricular rhythm is a slow, wide-complex back-up rhythm from the ventricles. Learn the rates, how AIVR differs, and why context decides how serious it is.
- [Junctional Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-rhythm/): In a junctional rhythm the AV junction takes over as pacemaker at 40–60 bpm. Learn how it is recognised, why it happens, and when it needs treatment.
- [Junctional Tachycardia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-tachycardia/): Junctional tachycardia is a fast rhythm from the AV junction, above 100 bpm, with absent or inverted P waves. Learn the causes and why digoxin toxicity is classic.
- [Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/multifocal-atrial-tachycardia/): Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with three or more P wave shapes, linked to lung disease. Learn how it differs from AFib.
- [Sinus Bradycardia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-bradycardia/): Sinus bradycardia is a normal rhythm running slower than 60 bpm. Learn why it is common in fit people and during sleep, and which symptoms mean it needs attention.
- [Sinus Pause and Sinus Arrest: What They Mean](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-pause-arrest/): A sinus pause is a gap where the heart's pacemaker briefly stops firing. Learn how long is significant, the common causes, and when a pause needs a pacemaker.
- [Sinus Rhythm With PACs: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm-with-pac/): 'Sinus rhythm with PACs' means a normal rhythm with occasional early beats from the upper chambers. Learn why they happen, what they feel like and when they matter.
- [Sinus Rhythm With Sinus Arrhythmia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-arrhythmia/): Despite the alarming name, sinus arrhythmia is a normal variation of heart rate with breathing. Here's why it happens and why it is a sign of a healthy heart.
- [Sinus Rhythm: What It Means on Your ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm/): Sinus rhythm is the normal heartbeat. What the term means, the numbers behind it, and what the added words (with PACs, 1st degree AV block) mean.
- [Sinus Tachycardia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-tachycardia/): Sinus tachycardia is a normal rhythm above 100 bpm — usually the heart responding to something. See the common triggers and when a fast rate needs checking.
- [Trigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/trigeminy/): Trigeminy is a repeating pattern in which every third heartbeat is an extra beat. Find out what causes it, whether it is dangerous and how doctors assess it.
- [Wandering Atrial Pacemaker: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wandering-atrial-pacemaker/): Wandering atrial pacemaker is a usually benign rhythm where the pacemaker site shifts and the P wave changes shape. Learn how it differs from MAT.

## Heart Blocks & Conduction
- [AV Blocks and Bundle Branch Blocks](https://www.ecgmeans.com/heart-block-conduction/): First, second and third degree AV block, left and right bundle branch block, and fascicular block — which are harmless and which are not.
- [2:1 AV Block: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/2-1-av-block/): In 2:1 AV block every other P wave is blocked. It can be the benign Mobitz I type or the more serious Mobitz II type. Learn how doctors tell them apart.
- [Intraventricular Conduction Delay (IVCD): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/intraventricular-conduction-delay/): A nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay is a wide QRS that is not a typical bundle branch block. Learn the common causes and when it needs assessment.
- [Left Anterior Fascicular Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-anterior-fascicular-block/): Left anterior fascicular block, or left anterior hemiblock, is a minor conduction delay that causes left axis deviation. Learn why it is usually harmless.
- [Left Bundle Branch Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-bundle-branch-block/): Left bundle branch block means the left side of the heart's wiring is delayed. Learn what it implies, why a new LBBB is taken seriously, and what tests follow.
- [Left Posterior Fascicular Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-posterior-fascicular-block/): Left posterior fascicular block is an uncommon conduction delay causing right axis deviation. Because the fascicle is sturdy, it often signals real disease.
- [Right Bundle Branch Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-bundle-branch-block/): Right bundle branch block (complete or incomplete) is a common ECG finding. What the rSR' pattern means and why incomplete RBBB is usually a normal variant.
- [Second Degree AV Block Type 1 (Wenckebach): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-1/): Mobitz I (Wenckebach) is second degree AV block where the PR interval lengthens until a beat drops. Why it is usually benign and how it differs from Type 2.
- [Second Degree AV Block Type 2 (Mobitz II): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-2/): Mobitz II is second degree AV block in which beats drop suddenly with a constant PR interval. Learn why it is taken seriously and why a pacemaker is usually advised.
- [Sinus Rhythm With 1st Degree AV Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/first-degree-av-block/): First degree AV block means the signal from the atria to the ventricles is slightly delayed (PR over 200 ms). Learn why it is usually benign and when it matters.
- [Third Degree (Complete) Heart Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/third-degree-av-block/): Complete heart block means no signals pass from the atria to the ventricles, which beat on their own escape rhythm. Learn why it usually needs an urgent pacemaker.

## Intervals & Waves
- [ECG Intervals and Waves: Normal Ranges](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-intervals-waves/): PR, QRS and QT/QTc normal ranges, what short and long values mean, and the T wave, ST segment and U wave changes that ECG reports mention.
- [Biphasic T Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/biphasic-t-wave/): A biphasic T wave goes both up and down. Depending on the pattern it can mean low potassium, ischaemia (Wellens), or be a minor finding. Learn how it is read.
- [Delta Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/delta-wave/): A delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS, the signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White. Learn what it means, the risks, and when it needs treatment.
- [Electrical Alternans: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/electrical-alternans/): Electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat change in the height of the QRS. Its classic cause is a large fluid collection around the heart. Learn when it is urgent.
- [Osborn Wave (J Wave): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/osborn-wave/): An Osborn wave (J wave) is a notch at the end of the QRS, classically caused by hypothermia. Learn what it looks like, its causes, and why it resolves on warming.
- [Peaked T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/peaked-t-waves/): Tall, peaked T waves can be a normal variant or an early warning of high potassium. Learn how to tell them apart and why new peaked T waves need prompt testing.
- [PR Interval: Normal Range and What Short or Long Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pr-interval/): The PR interval measures conduction from atria to ventricles. Normal is 120–200 ms. See what a short or prolonged PR means and the common causes of each.
- [QRS Interval: Normal Range and What a Wide QRS Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qrs-interval/): The QRS interval shows how long the ventricles take to activate. Normal is under 120 ms. Learn what a wide QRS means and the main reasons it happens.
- [QT and QTc Interval: Normal Range and Prolonged QT](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qt-interval/): The QTc is the heart-rate-corrected QT interval. Normal is under 440–460 ms. Learn why a long QTc matters, which medicines lengthen it, and what happens next.
- [S1Q3T3: What the Pattern Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/s1q3t3/): S1Q3T3 is an ECG pattern linked with pulmonary embolism, but it is neither sensitive nor specific. Learn what it is, why it happens, and how PE is really diagnosed.
- [Short PR Interval: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/short-pr-interval/): A short PR interval (under 120 ms) means the ventricles are being activated early. Learn about accessory pathways, WPW, and when a short PR is a normal variant.
- [ST Depression: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-depression/): ST depression means the ST segment sits below the baseline. It can signal reduced blood flow to the heart, or be caused by strain, digoxin or a fast heart rate.
- [ST Elevation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-elevation/): ST elevation can signal a heart attack (STEMI) but also has harmless causes like early repolarization and pericarditis. Learn what separates them.
- [T Wave Inversion: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/t-wave-inversion/): Inverted T waves can be normal in some leads and important in others. Learn where T wave inversion is expected, which patterns matter, and how it is assessed.
- [U Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/u-wave/): A U wave is a small bump after the T wave. Small U waves are normal; prominent U waves can signal low potassium or certain medicines. Learn when it matters.

## Comparisons
- [ECG Comparisons: This vs That](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-comparisons/): Side-by-side answers to the ECG questions patients ask most: PVC vs PAC, SVT vs VT, and EKG vs echocardiogram, explained in plain English.
- [EKG vs Echocardiogram: What's the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ekg-vs-echocardiogram/): An EKG records the heart's electrical activity; an echocardiogram is an ultrasound of its structure. What each shows, when each is used, and why you may need both.
- [PVC vs PAC: What's the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pvc-vs-pac/): PACs and PVCs are both extra heartbeats. See how they differ in origin, ECG appearance, symptoms and significance, and which one is more likely to need follow-up.
- [SVT vs VTach: What's the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/svt-vs-vtach/): SVT and ventricular tachycardia are both fast rhythms but differ in origin, ECG appearance and danger. Learn how doctors tell them apart and how each is treated.

## ECG Basics
- [ECG Basics for Patients](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-basics/): How to read the report in your hand, what a normal ECG can and cannot tell you, and the questions worth asking.
- [How to Read Your ECG Report: A Plain-English Guide](https://www.ecgmeans.com/how-to-read-ecg-report/): A step-by-step guide to the numbers and phrases printed on a 12-lead ECG report — rate, PR, QRS, QT/QTc, axis, the machine's findings and its overall verdict.
- [If My ECG Is Normal, Is My Heart OK?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/if-ecg-is-normal-is-my-heart-ok/): A normal ECG is reassuring for rhythm and acute damage but cannot rule out every heart problem. Learn what a normal ECG does and doesn't tell you.
- [What Is an EKG (ECG)? A Plain-English Guide](https://www.ecgmeans.com/what-is-an-ekg/): An EKG (ECG) is a quick, painless test of your heart's electrical activity. What it shows, what the letters mean, how long it takes and what it costs.

## ECG Tools & Calculators
- [ECG Tools and Calculators](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-tools/): Free ECG calculators for patients and students: QTc calculator, heart rate from an ECG, QRS axis calculator and a chart of normal adult ECG values.
- [ECG Axis Calculator](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-axis-calculator/): Free ECG axis calculator. Enter the net QRS size in leads I and aVF to get the electrical axis in degrees and see if it is normal, left or right axis deviation.
- [How to Calculate Heart Rate on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-heart-rate-calculator/): Calculate heart rate from an ECG with the 300, 1500 and 6-second methods. Free calculator using small boxes, large boxes, R-wave count or the RR interval.
- [Normal ECG Values (Adults)](https://www.ecgmeans.com/normal-ecg-values/): Normal adult ECG values in one chart: heart rate, P wave, PR, QRS, QT/QTc, axis, ST segment and T waves, with what it means when a value is outside range.
- [QTc Calculator (Corrected QT Interval)](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qtc-calculator/): Free QTc calculator. Enter the QT interval and heart rate to get the corrected QT by Bazett, Fridericia, Framingham and Hodges, with normal ranges explained.

## About
- [About ECG Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/about/): Who writes and reviews ECG Means, how each page is researched and medically reviewed, the references we use, and how to report a correction.
- [Privacy Policy](https://www.ecgmeans.com/privacy/): How ECG Means handles your data: no accounts, no health data collected, in-browser search and calculators, and Google AdSense advertising cookies.
- [Medical Disclaimer](https://www.ecgmeans.com/disclaimer/): ECG Means provides general educational information about ECG findings only. It is not medical advice and cannot interpret your individual ECG.
- [Contact](https://www.ecgmeans.com/contact/): Contact ECG Means to report a correction, suggest an ECG report phrase we should explain, or ask about the site. We cannot interpret individual ECGs.
